title: Visitors Flock to China's Sacred Wudang Mountains
paragraphs: Rising from the hills of Hubei Province in central China, the Wudang Mountains have been regarded as sacred for well over a thousand years. Today, they attract millions of people annually, ranging from devout pilgrims to sightseers and, increasingly, foreigners eager to immerse themselves in traditional Chinese culture.

The range comprises 72 peaks, all of which are said to converge toward Tianzhu Peak, where a bronze Taoist temple known as the Golden Hall stands at an altitude of roughly 1,610 meters. Wudang's Taoist buildings date back to the seventh century and were expanded substantially under subsequent dynasties. In particular, the Ming emperor Zhu Di commissioned an ambitious construction campaign intended to associate his rule with Taoism, at the same time as his Forbidden City was being built in Beijing. Today, more than 60 sites survive, and the ancient building complex was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1994. Taoist priests, recognizable by their high hair buns and blue robes, continue to look after the temples.

According to government figures, the sites received 14 million visits in 2025. Many visitors come to pray. One woman, who had traveled from Hebei Province with her daughter to pray for favorable weather and national prosperity, told the Associated Press that "This place watches over our country." Another visitor had come from Inner Mongolia to pray for her child's success at school.

Wudang is also renowned as one of Taoism's four sacred mountains and as the birthplace of Wudang tai chi, and this reputation is drawing growing numbers of foreigners. According to local tourism agencies, foreign visitor numbers rose by 70% in 2025 to 22,283, and by mid-June 2026, overseas arrivals were up 51% compared with the previous year. Most come from the United States, Canada and several European countries.

Notably, many of these visitors are not merely sightseeing but staying to study. While interest was once inspired largely by kung fu films, many now seek physical and mental well-being. Gu Shining, who heads a local martial arts academy, noted that "Tai Chi is the most popular and easiest to learn."
